article_title: Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce through Teacher Apprenticeships
citation: Nathan Kriha, Diarese George, Jonathan Feinstein, and Anna Skubel. (2025). Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce Through Teacher Apprenticeships. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Registered Teacher Apprenticeship Programs (RTAPs) and the National Guidelines for Apprenticeship Standards
description: RTAPs are a form of registered apprenticeship recognized by the U.S. Department of Labor in which apprentices hold paid positions with progressively increasing wages, complete at least 2,000 hours of structured on-the-job training under an experienced mentor, receive supplemental classroom instruction, and earn a portable, nationally recognized credential. The Pathways Alliance's National Guidelines add teacher-specific elements: competency-based completion, at least one academic year of on-the-job learning with a mentor-teacher at a ratio not exceeding two apprentices per mentor, at least 144 hours of related technical instruction, and no service as teacher of record. The report describes RTAPs as an "earn and learn" model intended to make teaching more accessible and affordable and to attract a more diverse candidate pool.
requirements: Programs must be registered with the U.S. Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency and operate as partnerships between districts and educator preparation programs
constraints: The report notes little research exists on the efficacy of these programs to produce high-quality, well-prepared, and diverse educators, and many programs have yet to graduate any apprentices
target_learners: adult learners and currently employed non-teacher school staff such as paraprofessionals and long-term substitutes seeking teacher licensure
target_learning_goals: full state teacher certification or licensure through competency-based, job-embedded educator preparation
examples: Programs studied in Tennessee and Texas placed apprentices in schools four to five days per week while completing coursework at night and on weekends, lasting one to three years depending on entry credentials
key_sources: Nathan Kriha, Diarese George, Jonathan Feinstein, and Anna Skubel. (2025). Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce Through Teacher Apprenticeships. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED678833

article_title: Self-efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real-time collaboration system developed for group programming
citation: Ting-Chia Hsu, Hal Abelson, Evan Patton, Shih-Chu Chen, Hsuan-Ning Chang. (2021). Self-efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real-time collaboration system developed for group programming. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09357-3
title: Instantly shared annotations and a chat room in RTC support constructing shared knowledge in multi-user programming
description: In the RTC environment, the annotation behavior (OI) became a channel for actively disseminating ideas about the co-created program: after a teammate read annotations, they returned to Designer to add a component (DCR). The authors map this onto Sun et al.'s first indicator of collaborative problem solving, "constructing shared knowledge", and conclude that "instantly sharing annotations or comments can be regarded as an important function in RTC."
requirements: Teammates must read annotations in the shared environment for the interaction sequence OI→DCR to occur
constraints: During individual programming, annotations were used only for the user's own later reading with no significant follow-on action; the principle applies to the collaborative RTC setting
target_learners: adult learners collaborating on block-based programming across CS and non-CS backgrounds
target_learning_goals: constructing shared knowledge and coordinating team programming work
examples: Teammates returned to the Designer environment to add components (DCR) after reading annotations (OI), forming a significant behavior pattern in multi-user programming
key_sources: Ting-Chia Hsu, Hal Abelson, Evan Patton, Shih-Chu Chen, Hsuan-Ning Chang. (2021). Self-efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real-time collaboration system developed for group programming. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09357-3

article_title: Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries
citation: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6
title: Redesigned TALIS-PISA Link (rTPL) database linking teacher and student data from the same schools
description: The rTPL is a linked database combining TALIS 2013 mathematics teacher responses with PISA 2012 student responses from the same schools, using the shared anchor variable PISASCHOOLID. The article states "The TPL dataset builds on data from 3473 teachers and 31,584 students in 1115 schools" across the participating countries, with per-country samples in its Table 2. The study uses it to measure mathematics instructional quality from both teacher and student perspectives in the same schools; only mathematics-teacher TPL data were linked to PISA student data.
requirements: Linking depends on the shared anchor variable PISASCHOOLID present in both TALIS 2013 and PISA 2012, which the article notes is available only for these two cycles.
constraints: The article cautions that because PISA 2012 and TALIS 2013 were not originally designed to study mathematics instructional quality or its psychometric properties, results should be interpreted with care and viewed as a general screening.
target_learning_goals: measuring the multidimensional construct of mathematics instructional quality from teacher and student perspectives
examples: For each country in the TALIS-PISA Link study, 150 schools, all eligible mathematics teachers, and 20 non-mathematics teachers participated.
key_sources: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Preschoolers identified for Tier II within an RTI framework need more intensive and more narrowly focused instruction than children at general risk
description: The article's central design recommendation is that the population identified for Tier II instruction matters. Children who fail to progress under a high-quality, evidence-based Tier I curriculum represent a more difficult-to-remediate group, so the authors conclude that "Children identified as eligible for Tier II in an RTI framework likely require more intensive and more narrowly focused instruction than do children at general risk of later academic difficulties." The two studies support this: broad-scope Tier II activities with prior efficacy evidence produced minimal impacts in Study 1, while the intensified, narrowed Study 2 version produced significant impacts.
requirements: Tier I must first be a high-quality, evidence-based core curriculum so that Tier II identification reflects genuine non-response rather than weak core instruction
constraints: Evidence comes from Title I preschool settings with children averaging standard scores of roughly 78 to 86 at qualification; the authors state the context of identification may alter the nature of Tier II instruction required
target_learners: preschool children who fail to make adequate progress under evidence-based core classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: early literacy skills: phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language
examples: After Study 1's minimal impacts, the authors revised the protocols to be more intensive, more focused, and more explicit, and Study 2 showed significant and moderate-to-large impacts
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Response to instruction in preschool: Results of two randomized studies with children at significant risk of reading difficulties.
citation: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054
title: Response to Instruction (RTI) three-tier framework for organizing instructional intensity
description: The article describes RTI as two interrelated approaches: a method for identifying learning disabilities via universal screening, risk identification, increasing instructional intensity, and progress monitoring; and a framework of tiers of instructional intensity. In the standard three-tiered model, "Tier II represents an increased intensity of instruction, often administered as small-group instruction, with membership in the small-groups differentiated by students' skill levels", while Tier III provides even smaller-group or one-on-one instruction often delivered by specialists. Tier I is the core, evidence-based classroom instruction expected to meet 75 to 90 percent of children.
requirements: Universal screening and frequent progress monitoring with curriculum-based measures; a core Tier I curriculum that is high-quality and evidence-based
constraints: The article notes it is not clear the high-quality Tier I presumption is met in many preschool classrooms, where most commonly used curricula lack WWC evidence of efficacy
target_learners: preschool and elementary children at risk of academic difficulties
target_learning_goals: early identification and remediation of academic skill deficits, particularly early literacy
examples: The studies operationalized Tier II as 11 weeks of need-aligned small-group instruction in phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language strands, randomized against Tier I only
key_sources: Lonigan, C. J., & Phillips, B. M. (2016). Response to Instruction in Preschool: Results of Two Randomized Studies with Children At Significant Risk of Reading Difficulties. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000054

article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Six design dimensions with 12 research questions for the RTS design space
description: The paper organizes the design space of reciprocal tutoring systems into six dimensions, each posing research questions that assist developers in adopting the CLS approach. The dimensions are task partition, social scaffolding, scaffolding tools, scaffolding and fading, student modeling, and benefit-cost-tradeoffs. The authors state: They are divided into six design dimensions: task partition (questions #1 and #2), social scaffolding (questions #3 and #4), scaffolding tools (questions #5 and #6), scaffolding and fading (questions #7, #8, and #9), student modeling (questions #10 and #11), and benefit-cost-tradeoffs (question #12). Although focused on reciprocal tutoring, they note the questions and principles can be applied to other learning activities.
requirements: Designers must analyze how the learning task is decomposed, which brain performs which part of the learning task, and how these brains should interact
constraints: Involving as many CLS mechanisms as possible may not lead to a good RTS
target_learners: Students in reciprocal tutoring arrangements in one-to-one classrooms
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-tutoring and learning-by-being-tutored
examples: Table 1 compares the designs of related RTSs according to the design space, listing configurations, companions, tasks, reciprocity, and scaffolding tools of systems from Integration-Kid to OPAL
key_sources: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7

article_title: Response to Intervention: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See. (2014). Response to Intervention: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Response to Intervention (RTI) tiered literacy programme with needs analysis, intervention menu and progress tracking tools
description: RTI is a targeted, tiered approach to identifying the needs of low-achieving pupils: "a whole class approach as preventive teaching (Tier 1), followed by small group remediation (Tier 2)" and one-to-one tutoring (Tier 3) for those who do not respond to small group instruction. In this evaluation CUREE developed the tools, resources and training, supported by AfA3As Achievement Coaches. Key elements include needs analysis via a Close-case Analysis Tool, a menu of research-based interventions for different literacy areas, and Tracking Pupil Progress Tools used at mid-intervention and end-of-intervention points.
requirements: Teachers trained to use the diagnostic and tracking tools; identification of eligible pupils using pre-test results, teacher judgement and the RTI diagnostic tool
constraints: Duration, intensity and frequency of treatment were allowed to vary from school to school; in this trial the summer-term timing limited delivery
target_learners: Year 6 pupils at risk of not achieving Level 4 English at Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: Literacy (reading, comprehension, spelling, vocabulary, phonics, fluency)
examples: Teachers used the Close-case Analysis Tool to set tier intensity and chose from a menu including Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies, inference training, repeated reading and embedded phonics
key_sources: Stephen Gorard, Nadia Siddiqui, Beng Huat See. (2014). Response to Intervention: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581264

article_title: Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy
citation: Merav W. Efrat. (2017). Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy. Contemporary Issues in Education Research, 10(2). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/cier
title: Recess Time Physical Activity Self-Efficacy Scale (RTPASES)
description: The RTPASES is Efrat's (2016) instrument measuring children's recess-time physical activity self-efficacy, adapted from prior physical activity self-efficacy scales. It "measured three types of task self-efficacy (vigorous, moderate, and light) and two types of physical activity barrier self-efficacy (adult encouragement barrier self-efficacy and other barrier self-efficacy)" on a 5-point Likert scale from not at all confident to definitely confident. In this study it was administered with comprehension-support activities such as concrete activity examples and brief bouts at each intensity.
requirements: Administered with supports the article describes: verbal descriptions of activity intensities, brief bouts at each intensity, and a chalk-line confidence-jumping task to verify children understand the scale descriptors
constraints: Baseline data and instrument were drawn from a previously published study (Efrat, 2016)
target_learning_goals: confidence to engage in light, moderate, and vigorous physical activity during recess
confidence to overcome barriers to recess physical activity
examples: Before administering the scale, participants sprinted a short distance after hearing the definition of vigorous physical activity, and rated confidence to jump to five chalk-marked distances
key_sources: Merav W. Efrat. (2017). Exploring Strategies That Influence Children's Physical Activity Self-Efficacy. Contemporary Issues in Education Research, 10(2). https://clutejournals.com/index.php/cier

article_title: Response to Intervention: Research and Practice
citation: Carol Hall, Jamie Mahoney. (2013). Response To Intervention: Research And Practice. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 6(3). https://www.clutejournals.com
title: Response to Intervention as a pre-referral service delivery model
description: Response to Intervention (RTI) is a service model "designed to meet the learning needs of students prior to diagnosis and placement in special education settings". It uses universal screening to identify struggling students early so the general education teacher can provide remediation using the regular curriculum supplemented with additional instructional resources, preventing over-representation, misidentification, and labeling of students as learning disabled. The model merges accountability practices of general and special education teachers to ensure students make academic progress, and is supported through IDEIA. The article studies how teachers implement this model in practice.
requirements: General education teachers implementing remediation with regular curriculum plus additional instructional resources
Early identification before referral for special education services
constraints: The article reports that extensive staff development at demonstration sites did not improve teachers' self-reported implementation of the model in the studied district
target_learners: students at risk of misidentification as learning disabled
target_learning_goals: early identification and remediation of academic skill deficits
preventing unnecessary special education referral
examples: A Florida district implemented an RTI plan with demonstration schools receiving extensive professional development, compared against comparable schools
key_sources: Carol Hall, Jamie Mahoney. (2013). Response To Intervention: Research And Practice. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 6(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1073194

article_title: A Written Language Intervention for At-Risk Second Grade Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial of the Process Assessment of the Learner Lesson Plans in a Tier 2 Response-to-Intervention (RtI) Model
citation: Hooper, S. R., Costa, L.-J. C., McBee, M., Anderson, K. L., Yerby, D. C., Childress, A., & Knuth, S. B. (2013). A written language intervention for at-risk second grade students: a randomized controlled trial of the process assessment of the learner lesson plans in a tier 2 response-to-intervention (RtI) model. Ann. of Dyslexia, 63, 44-64. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11881-011-0056-y
title: Response-to-intervention (RtI) three-tier framework
description: RtI is described as "a prevention oriented approach to learning needs wherein there are direct links from assessment to instruction", with regular ongoing progress monitoring. Its three tiers are "early intervention for prevention of problems for all learners (Tier 1), curriculum modifications for at-risk learners (Tier 2), and instructional treatment for students with specific disabilities (Tier 3)", with Tier 2 typically delivered in small groups. The article stresses RtI is a framework, not an instructional program, and used a Tier 2 small-group format to deliver the PAL lesson plans.
requirements: Evidence-based interventions as a central part of selecting treatments; direct assessment strategies informing instruction
constraints: The article cites concerns about RtI strategies raised by Reynolds and Shaywitz (2009) while reporting modest support for Tier 2 utility
target_learners: all elementary students, with Tier 2 for at-risk learners
target_learning_goals: prevention and remediation of academic skill deficits, here written expression
examples: All first graders were screened with the WIAT-II Written Expression Subtest, and at-risk students received small-group Tier 2 intervention between February and May of second grade
key_sources: Hooper, S. R., Costa, L.-J. C., McBee, M., Anderson, K. L., Yerby, D. C., Childress, A., & Knuth, S. B. (2013). A written language intervention for at-risk second grade students: a randomized controlled trial of the process assessment of the learner lesson plans in a tier 2 response-to-intervention (RtI) model. Ann. of Dyslexia, 63, 44-64. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11881-011-0056-y

article_title: Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study.
citation: Siu Yikchi, Bai Hefei, Yoon Jung-Min, Ye Hongqiang, Liu Yunsong, Zhou Yongsheng. (2025). Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71743
title: RTS (Yikchi Siu): participatory 3D simulation software for preclinical RPD framework design training
description: RTS is a standalone Windows program developed in Visual Studio Code that simulates the clinical process of treating patients with partial edentulism. It contains "3D digital casts created from clinical plaster casts from 19 dental patients" and organizes training into 5 topics: clinical examination, cast surveying, RPD framework design, design scoring, and answer and explanation. Users survey casts digitally, design frameworks with abutment teeth, clasps, rests, and connectors, and receive automatic scoring with immediate feedback; a score of 60 or above unlocks the standardized design and explanation, otherwise the case must be redesigned.
requirements: Users must open the provided URL, register, and log in; each training mode contains 6 to 7 practice cases that must all be completed before the next mode unlocks
constraints: The surveying function cannot replace a physical surveyor: the article states it "demonstrates poorer adaptability for complex cases" and is designed solely to provide preliminary practice in understanding model survey angles
target_learners: newly enrolled stomatology master's students without preclinical RPD training
target_learning_goals: RPD framework design
cast surveying
Kennedy classification
clinical decision-making in prosthodontics
examples: In the training phase (September 2024 to October 2024), 26 newly enrolled postgraduate students used the system, which was assessed quantitatively via test scores and qualitatively via questionnaires
key_sources: Siu Yikchi, Bai Hefei, Yoon Jung-Min, Ye Hongqiang, Liu Yunsong, Zhou Yongsheng. (2025). Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71743

article_title: Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study.
citation: Siu Yikchi, Bai Hefei, Yoon Jung-Min, Ye Hongqiang, Liu Yunsong, Zhou Yongsheng. (2025). Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71743
title: Five-topic participatory simulation cycle with gated practice modes and automatic scoring with feedback
description: The RTS instructional pattern sequences training through "clinical examination, cast surveying, RPD framework design, design scoring, and answer and explanation". Practice modes are gated: all cases in a mode must be successfully completed before the next mode unlocks. After design submission, the system automatically scores the work and provides immediate feedback including a standardized design for comparison; scores below 60 require redesigning the case. Faculty can also review and manually grade designs in the background.
requirements: 3D digital casts reviewed and approved for relevance and accuracy by prosthodontics experts; an evaluation system providing automatic scoring and immediate feedback
constraints: Gating requires successful completion of each case; a system score below 60 forces the case to be designed again
target_learning_goals: RPD framework design skills
self-directed practice with feedback
examples: Figure 3 shows a Kennedy classification III case exercise in which the user rotates the 3D cast, determines the Kennedy type, surveys the inverted concave area, designs the framework, and submits it for automatic scoring
key_sources: Siu Yikchi, Bai Hefei, Yoon Jung-Min, Ye Hongqiang, Liu Yunsong, Zhou Yongsheng. (2025). Enhancing Preclinical Training for Removable Partial Dentures Through Participatory 3D Simulation: Development and Usability Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71743

article_title: Low Frequency, High Complexity: Assessing Skill Decay in Transesophageal Echocardiography Post-Simulation Training.
citation: Ablordeppey E, Terian E, Murray CT, Wallace L, Huang W, Blustein E, Croft A, Romo E, Agarwal M, Theodoro D. (2025). Low Frequency, High Complexity: Assessing Skill Decay in Transesophageal Echocardiography Post-Simulation Training. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.35857
title: Multimodal rTEE training curriculum with monthly criterion-based proficiency simulator sessions
description: A pilot curriculum combining clinical introduction (observing clinical rTEEs with supervised probe manipulation), asynchronous web-based didactics, and monthly hands-on sessions on the HeartWorks rTEE high-fidelity simulator. Training was "organized into clinical introduction, synchronous didactics, and simulator training," with proficiency defined as errorless acquisition of eight adequate rTEE views on cue, and training continued for four months even after proficiency was met.
requirements: A board-certified rTEE instructor who assesses proficiency monthly via direct observation
A high-fidelity rTEE simulator and access to clinical rTEE observation for the clinical introduction component
constraints: The article notes the simulator may be easier than clinical practice due to absence of complications like probe insertion or chest compression motion, and should be viewed as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for hands-on training
target_learners: rTEE-naive emergency physicians proficient in transthoracic echocardiography
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and retention of eight resuscitative transesophageal echocardiography views, including naming, probe manipulation, and image acquisition
examples: Seven emergency physicians trained monthly for four months until all reached the full proficiency score of 32 on the checklist-based assessment tool
key_sources: Ablordeppey E, Terian E, Murray CT, Wallace L, Huang W, Blustein E, Croft A, Romo E, Agarwal M, Theodoro D. (2025). Low Frequency, High Complexity: Assessing Skill Decay in Transesophageal Echocardiography Post-Simulation Training. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.35857

article_title: Defining competence profiles in obstetrics and gynecology using the modified requirement tracking questionnaire.
citation: Tarasi Baptiste, Oubaid Viktor, Baud David. (2025). Defining competence profiles in obstetrics and gynecology using the modified requirement tracking questionnaire. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06806-7
title: Modified requirement-tracking questionnaire (R-track) for assessing professional competence profiles
description: The R-track is a job-analysis questionnaire inspired by the Fleishman Job Analysis Survey, originally developed for aviation and aerospace and later adapted for physicians. The French version used here contains 66 items across eight competence areas — "Mental abilities", "Social sensibility", "Psychomotor and multitasking abilities", "Solutions orientation", "Social interactive competences", "Personality traits", "Verbal competences" and "Resistance capacity" — rated on a 5-point Likert scale of importance for daily professional activity. The authors chose it because personality traits and social-interactive competencies are only superficially addressed by the FJAS and it offers "a psychologically comprehensive assessment of the necessary characteristics, competencies, and skills".
requirements: Respondents rate each of the 66 items on a 5-point Likert scale from very low to very high importance for daily professional activity; mean scores of single items and competence areas are then calculated
constraints: The study used a French-translated version distributed in French-speaking Switzerland; the authors note results from this local sample can only be generalized with caution
target_learners: physicians in obstetrics and gynecology at all training levels
target_learning_goals: defining competence profiles for residency selection
career-choice guidance for medical specialties
examples: Sent to 307 physicians via mailing list with 201 responses; item and area means ranked in Table 1 and Supplements 2–3
key_sources: Tarasi Baptiste, Oubaid Viktor, Baud David. (2025). Defining competence profiles in obstetrics and gynecology using the modified requirement tracking questionnaire. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06806-7

article_title: Training with virtual patients in transcultural psychiatry: do the learners actually learn?
citation: Pantziaras I, Fors U, Ekblad S. (2015). Training With Virtual Patients in Transcultural Psychiatry: Do the Learners Actually Learn? Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3497
title: Refugee Trauma Simulation (RT-SIM): a virtual patient system for transcultural psychiatry training
description: The Refugee Trauma Simulation is a virtual patient system that "portrays an adult Bosnian refugee" (“Mrs K.”) with severe symptoms of PTSD and major depression. Learners conduct a video-based medical interview by selecting questions from category lists, physically examine the patient, order laboratory and imaging tests, and complete a preliminary assessment covering history, differential diagnosis, and treatment plan. The article evaluated its impact on the knowledge of 32 resident psychiatrists.
requirements: Learners "interact with the VP for up to 45 minutes as they would in a real-life clinical encounter"
constraints: The evaluated system portrays a single case: an adult Bosnian refugee with severe PTSD and major depression symptoms
target_learning_goals: PTSD diagnostic criteria and clinical management
clinical reasoning, decision making, and history taking
basic communication skills
examples: Residents completed a pre-interaction and post-interaction knowledge test around one session with the system
key_sources: Pantziaras I, Fors U, Ekblad S. (2015). Training With Virtual Patients in Transcultural Psychiatry: Do the Learners Actually Learn? Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3497

article_title: Educational potential of a virtual patient system for caring for traumatized patients in primary care.
citation: Ekblad Solvig, Mollica Richard F, Fors Uno, Pantziaras Ioannis, Lavelle James. (2013). Educational potential of a virtual patient system for caring for traumatized patients in primary care. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-110
title: RTSim: a Refugee Trauma Simulator with video-based interview, screening instruments, and dual feedback
description: RTSim is a virtual patient system for training primary care professionals to manage traumatized refugee patients. Its prototype supports six interaction areas: medical interview, physical examination including mental status examination, screening instruments (HTQ, HSCL-25, PHQ-2, PHQ-9 and others), laboratory tests and imaging, additional data, and preliminary assessment with treatment plan. The interview uses video clips of a Bosnian actor recorded in Bosnian and subtitled in English, and after the encounter the learner receives feedback from the virtual refugee herself and from a virtual advisor (domain expert).
requirements: Learners need internet access and sufficient IT proficiency to run the on-line system; participants with "poor" internet skills were excluded from invitation
constraints: The current version does not allow free-text open-ended questions, which participants missed; feedback from the VP and virtual advisor was reported as not totally clear and needing technical improvement; the physical examination module was seen as limited
target_learning_goals: interviewing and assessing traumatized refugee patients
use of trauma and mental health screening instruments
diagnosis and treatment planning for comorbid health and mental health problems
examples: 11 PCPs at Lynn Community Health Centre completed three 60-75 minute sessions: introduction with pre-test, independent encounter with the virtual refugee, and a follow-up interview one month later
key_sources: Ekblad Solvig, Mollica Richard F, Fors Uno, Pantziaras Ioannis, Lavelle James. (2013). Educational potential of a virtual patient system for caring for traumatized patients in primary care. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-110
